title: 36. Being Young AND the Best Version of Yourself feat. Sarah Humphrey
description_html: This week I am joined by Sarah Humphrey, the host of It Ain't It Sis. We talk bullying, body image, struggling with mental health at a young age, college advice, and so much more. To follow along with Sarah, you can listen to her podcast on every platform, follow her on Instagram (@sarahhumphrey7 and @it.aint.it.sis). Listen to the episode Sarah and I recorded together on her show here.

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Nevertheless, She Persisted. I'm your host, Sadie. Every Friday, I post interviews about mental health, dialectical behavioral therapy, and teenage life. These episodes break down my mental health journey, teach skills to help you cope with life, and showcase testimonials from teens just like you. Whether you've struggled yourself or just want to improve your mental fitness, this podcast is your inspiration to live a life you love and keep persisting.

Today's guest is Sarah Humphrey, a self-acclaimed life enthusiast and recent graduate of the University of San Diego. She's also the host of the It Ain't It Sis podcast, which is all about navigating redirections, personal development, and relationships. I invited her on the podcast to talk about her mental health journey and give her perspective on maintaining your mental health as a college student, her experience podcasting, and so much more. I hope you enjoy. Thank you so much for joining me on She Persisted today.

Of course. Thank you so much for having me, Sadie. I'm just so excited to be on. Me too. Okay. So I wanted to start our episode by hearing your mental health story. So starting with your teenage years, what was your journey with your mental health? Well, mental health for me is something that I've kind of always struggled with to a certain extent. When I was younger, especially in sixth grade, I was bullied a lot. And that's kind of when I started to notice I was struggling to be a little bit more happy compared to the other kids.

Growing up, I also would go to sometimes psychologists because I do have learning disabilities. And my psychologist would always tell me, she's like, you are a little bit more anxious than the normal child. Yeah. So I've always, since I was six, I think is when they first diagnosed me as anxious or having anxiety disorder. And so it's just something always I've dealt with. But, you know, as you kind of go on and go through life, things happen that kind of, I think, trigger your mental health. And so when I was 13 was when kind of like my depression and anxiety started to get really bad. Mm-hmm.

And then I was able to switch schools. So the bullying was able to stop, which was great. But also then kind of going into high school, that's when I started to really struggle with, I guess, body dysmorphia and body insecurity, which I know a lot of girls do these days. So easy to struggle with that kind of thing, especially with social media. Definitely. Yeah.

It's a thing that, I mean, we see all these girls, all these gorgeous girls who are very skinny, but we don't see a wide variety of many different body types. Yeah. And so I really took that to heart and I really struggled. I would say from the time I was 16 to about 20 years old, I'm 23 now, but 16 to 20 was...

a time that I really just struggled with my eating disorder. And then on top of that, when you are just so, I guess, consumed by the thoughts, then, you know, that triggers a lot of your anxiety and depression. And luckily I was able to get a lot of help and kind of, pushed through that. And now I'm kind of here on the other side. And even though I still do struggle with, you know, anxiety daily, I'm able to cope with it just due to like the therapy I've been through. So that's just like a little bit. Thank you. Yeah. That's just like a little bit in a nutshell of my mental health journey.

Yeah. So touching back on like the body dysmorphia and eating disorder kind of stuff, that's something that I've struggled with a lot. And it's definitely hard to find a good balance with of being healthy, but not letting it become obsessive. I'm someone where I'm either like, I'm just not going to pay attention to it at all because that's easier. Or I like kind of go down the path of being more obsessive or more anxious about what I'm intaking and how healthy I'm eating. So what have you found to be effective to stay healthy, but not become super obsessive

eating and body image and all of that? Yeah, I'm glad that you asked that question because it is very difficult to really fight those obsessive thoughts, especially just for like my personality type. I am very controlling. Yeah, me too. Yes. So I think especially people with those personality types, it is easier for you to kind of, fall into, I guess, the mindset of having an eating disorder. Not to say that everyone who is very controlling will fall into that mindset, but it is definitely easier. It's a more slippery slope for sure. Yeah, exactly. So I would say just over the years, what I've really taught myself is that it is okay to eat the cupcake if you really, really want one. It is okay to, I guess...

you know, just eat what you want and sometimes overeat and that's okay. Don't do it all the time, but you know, it's all about a balance. But one thing I actually would say that really helped me with kind of learning balance and not being so obsessive with everything that I kind of do in life is I went to Italy actually during my junior year. It was during my fall semester.

And during that time, I was really struggling with body dysmorphia too. I was really nervous about going because, I mean, when you think Italy, you just think carbs, wine, out late at night. And I'm thinking here in the back of my mind, I'm like... oh, that does not sound good to your waistline. Yeah, yeah, definitely. And I was like, okay, how is this going to work? And I was really just really nervous about going, but kind of going there really showed me that –

you know what, you can sometimes indulge, you can have that gelato, you can have some wine, you can eat pasta, pizza, or whatever. And you're still not gonna like gain 5 billion pounds, like I tell myself in my head. So I really kind of learned balance in going to Italy. And that's just one thing I just, I guess overall,

now understand that, you know what, you can live a balanced life when it comes to just being healthy and even going back to like body dysmorphia. I think that really helped me once I learned that, no, you can live a balanced life in terms of your eating and exercise habits. And that really, I think, shaped how I viewed my body in turn because now I'm understanding, okay,

What I do, it doesn't affect me as much as I think it does. Make it out to be. Definitely. It's the same thing for me. Once I got into more therapy, I learned that I'm always my own worst enemy and I make things out so much worse than they actually are, whether it's with eating or with how other people will perceive me or...

Just standards for myself. Like I put it so much worse than it is in reality. And so it's definitely important to take that step back and be like, okay, it's really not that bad. Like checking the facts, what is actually going to happen and kind of go easy on yourself, even though that's really, really difficult to do sometimes.

Yeah, no, exactly. And I liked how you touched on kind of just checking the facts. Because I think so often we are given so much information in this time, especially on social media. A lot of it isn't accurate. A lot of these people who claim to be health experts, while there is probably some truth in everything someone says,

It's not all truth. And I think it's so easy to remember or to, sorry, it's so easy to forget that these people giving advice are only people and they don't have it all figured out. And sometimes when you are a person who is insecure about their body and then you see someone saying, on the internet who has those six packs that you've always wanted it's so easy to be like oh they must know they must be correct yeah exactly they must know but you have to like take a step back and be like wait maybe they were honestly just blessed with that body and maybe yes they do put in the hard work and they do eat healthy but at the end of the day like a lot of it comes down to genetics and we just need to learn to be okay with that because at the end of

glorify every kind of body shape because it is such a terrible thought to just glorify one body and I think we find so much freedom and just letting that idea go that there is one perfect body type yeah yeah and you can really just find peace within that Yeah, and it's also like when you go and you look at someone who seems to have it all together as far as their health and their body image, what works for them may not work for you. And I think that that gets lost a lot that, again, it's down to genetics and we don't have the same genetics as the next person. So what's so effective for them is...

is almost guaranteed to not be as effective or impact you differently than it does for them. And that's definitely hard to remember because it's advertised as the fix-all and it's 100% going to work and stuff like that. And it's just not always the case. But yeah. I know. And then like, even when we get these advertisements for these skinny teas, I'm sure everyone's seen them and they claim, oh, it's a fix all or this diet pill is, you know, it'll flatten your tummy. In one day. Yeah. In one, in one day. And I'm like, that's not how it works. Yeah. Yeah. Sorry. No, you're good. Okay.

Yeah, but I'm like, that's not how it works at all. And I think we've just been preached this false reality for so long that health is... Just health is this one thing. And in reality, health is, it incorporates so many different things. Yeah. It is emotional health. It is mental health, spiritual health, physical health. It encompasses a wide range of things rather than just kind of, I think, the media is

puts it in a box and says, no, health is a skinny tea. Definitely. And I think one of the most amazing things about your mental health is once you get that on track and in place, your mental health, to maintain that, you have to be physically healthy. You have to be eating regularly and exercising and having positive relationships. There's all these little things that need to be

maintained for you to feel happy and joyful and have your mental health be thriving. And so once you get to that place, everything can kind of fall into place behind that. So that's something I love so much about working on your mental health is that it is such an abstract and broad concept, but it does really encompass all these other anxieties and worries that you have as well, because there's so many things you have to work on and maintain to be healthy mentally.

No, exactly. And just, I think a lot of people think working on their mental health is telling yourself, oh, I'm happy and just trying to achieve a certain level of happiness. I think that's what a lot of people think. mental health is. And I completely disagree because I think it is so important to feel all of those emotions because when we neglect, I guess, the different trials that we go through in life, whether it be just...

I guess like a breakup or a loss or you even failed a test or you didn't get the job you wanted, all of those things. I think a lot of people think mental health is kind of going through those things and being like, yeah, that happened, but it's okay. And I am a firm believer that you can kind of feel those emotions and

You can throw yourself like a little pity party for a couple minutes, but then you have to get over it is the point. You can't live in that pity party because that's when, you know, you get depressed and you get anxious and you get just kind of in the mindset of why is this all happening to me? Totally. But I think it's so important just on everyone's mental health journey that you really, you

You really just embrace all of the emotions that you're feeling regardless of what you're feeling because every feeling that you have is valid. Not everyone will understand it. Yeah. At the end of the day, what you're feeling is valid and it's okay. Yeah. And when you're not attending to those emotions like sadness or grief or anger, whatever it is, if you're just ignoring them, you're saying, you know what? No, I'm happy. Like, I love my life. This is good. It's just going to build up and compound more and more. And then you're not able to cope with it. So when you're attending to these different things you're experiencing as they arise, it's so much easier to cope than when they become so overwhelming. And you're like, I don't know how to deal with this. I've never felt an emotion this strong before. And you just don't know how to go forward. Yeah.

Exactly. And that's what I kind of noticed with a lot of people kind of close to me even where they just kind of bottle it up inside and they say constantly, it's okay. I'm fine. It's all okay. And yes, it is good to constantly give yourself pep talks and be like, I got this. It's fine. But yeah.

One thing I've also noticed is they don't really open up and being vulnerable is so incredibly important because that's how you kind of really release your emotions. And there is a quote that I saw today. I'm actually reading a great book. It's called Power to Persevere. I interviewed actually the author recently on my podcast and he's like,

And she's a cancer survivor, but she was telling me about kind of how vulnerability is actually a great strength because a lot of people think in order to be strong, you kind of have to shove down all of your emotions. But in reality, that's so not true because really being able to... Tell people, hey, this is how I'm feeling. I'm sad. I'm happy. I'm anxious. I'm whatever. That takes a lot of emotional strength to do. And I think when you're able to be vulnerable is when you're able to.

properly have emotional release and when you don't have emotional release that's when you get just the sudden outcries and yeah yeah like the little temper tantrums that you know just like blows up but you're like I don't know what to do with it yeah yeah exactly it's so funny because I think toddlers are known to have a lot of like

temper tantrums. But in reality, like, you can kind of see that in adults, too. Like, yeah, sure. They're not on the floor crying. I mean, maybe they are. I mean, we've all been there at some point. Yes. Yes. But... It's, I think vulnerability is a skill that we learn. And I mean, if you don't learn it, then you'll kind of just be one of those adults having these temper tantrums and you're not going to be able to know how to kind of cope with your emotions. So that's why I think vulnerability is so important to learn.

No, I completely agree. So switching gears a little bit, I wanted to ask about your college experience because you just graduated from University of San Diego. And a lot of listeners are teenagers are still in high school or just starting college or about to go into the application process. So first question is just overall experience. What were the highs, the lows? How was college for you?

Well, overall, I would say I really loved college. I had mentioned earlier that I was bullied and I was also bullied a lot in high school too. And it was so funny because the people who bullied me were actually a lot of guys and very typical, you know. Totally can relate. Yeah. Yeah, I hate that it's true, but a lot of younger guys, when they like you, I guess they make fun of you. Who knows why they do that? It doesn't work. It really doesn't work. But nevertheless, when I went to college was, I think, the first time I really felt like I was noticed. And that's exciting, obviously. And so I really loved college. I found a great group.

friends but kind of during that time I had experienced a lot of really traumatic moments I guess in terms of guys too I had been sexually assaulted a few different times and that especially in terms of just like really spiking my anxiety and depression and just a lot of self-doubt I think You know, it's a topic that a lot of people want to shy away from. Yeah. And I'm not afraid to talk about it. And sometimes, even though I am very cognizant of who I bring it up to because it is such a personal topic. But I think during my college years, that was something that kind of really weighed heavy on my heart. I mean...

To say that I didn't think about it every day would be a lie. But that being said, I remember this moment when I was talking to my mom. And I was crying to her just about everything that had happened in regards to, I guess, like... boys and all my experiences that were pretty negative. Yeah. But my mom, basically, she just reminded me that I need to kind of reframe how I view these experiences. And she really helped me like reframe my mindset in terms of just remembering that these experiences, yes, they are terrible, but you can always learn something. And yeah,

The whole saying, everything happens for a reason. I've heard actually an interesting argument. I'm not sure. Have you ever heard of Rachel Hollis? I haven't. No. Okay. She is one of my idols, honestly. She wrote a book, Girl, Wash Your Face. Okay. If you haven't read it, I would highly suggest to read it. I definitely will. But she was talking about how she had gone through a really traumatic

experience in her childhood and the whole idea around like everything happens for a reason. She didn't like that idea because she's like, there is sometimes no reason why people go through terrible experiences. There is no reason, but she kind of shifted her perspective and says, okay, maybe everything doesn't happen for a reason, but everything happens for a purpose.

And when I started kind of thinking about just my past experiences with like, by eating disorder, depression, anxiety, and sexual assault, and all of those things, they can really be deemed as negative. And yes, they are. But I'm a firm believer that everything happens for a purpose. And now I honestly feel like my life's purpose is to help other people struggling with those various things.

Yeah, no, I completely agree. When I was at such a low with my depression and my anxiety and my relationships and all of that, I didn't understand why it was happening to me. I was like, I'm 13, 14, however old I was at the time. And I was like, why? Why? I didn't know where to put the blame. I was like, why would God give me this life that is so miserable for me? What have I done to myself that's made this life so miserable? Why would my parents raise me into this life that I hate so much?

Like, I just didn't know why or where to shove this anger and resentment and all of this. And I did not see a reason. I didn't see a purpose in it. And it took years. It took probably four years for me to be like, okay, I've gotten past this really low, low that I've experienced in my life. And I, similar to you, see this purpose of...

I've been where these other teenagers have been and had a really unique insight into what they've gone through. And I can, through the podcast and hopefully later on in life, help them through that and help others who have struggled with their mental health. But it took coming out of that low and having that different vantage point to see that purpose. And so to anyone who hasn't gotten to that point yet or is still at that low and doesn't see the purpose, it's definitely fair to not...

to not feel like there's a reason and to not feel like there's a purpose because sometimes it takes time to be able to get to that vantage point where you can look back at it and really see the benefits to what you've gone through. Exactly. And that's why I also feel like I kind of resonate with you, especially just kind of growing up. I mean, to be honest, I really didn't like my life. I was really, yeah, exactly. I was just very bitter about it and I was really angry, kind of just...

I put the blame a lot of times on my parents, on myself, on God even. And I was like, why are girls my age kind of just going through life? Everything's fine. They can go to soccer practice and they can kind of eat whatever they want or they can just even be happy. They don't even have to try to be happy. And yeah.

I really kind of was bitter about that for a long time. And it's hard, especially when you are younger, going through those things and then seeing everyone around you. They kind of... talk a lot about, I know a lot of adults talk about how childhood you have a lot of kind of innocence and a lot of adults think. Children are, I guess, naive, but I completely disagree. Sometimes I think

children, I mean, are some of the most wise people I know. And just even what you were saying about experiencing those lows at 13. And I completely understand, like, I firmly, like, I say this all the time, not all the time, but when I tell people my story, I firmly believe that, I mean, my rock bottom, I've hit it probably like three different times in my life. But the first time was when I was 17 years old.

Yeah. And people are like, oh, usually I guess the 35 year olds, they'll hit rock bottom. And I'm like, no, just because I'm young doesn't mean I can't still experience these things. And I was bitter for kind of everything, or I was bitter with everything that was like happening in my life, just that I had experienced so much pain, but just really being able to.

to really shift my mindset and understand that, okay, I did experience all of these things at a very young age, but now I'm kind of shifting my mindset to being like, okay, well, this is kind of great for me because now I can really just go after what I'm passionate about. And that is helping children who are going through

certain situations. Now it can go after that when I'm still young and I still kind of get it and I'm still their age. Yeah. And it's like a gift kind of because you don't have to go through this giant journey of self-discovery and learning how to cope with your life because you already know how. So once you get into living your real life without your parents there to support you, without

this world you've grown up and known, once you're thrown into the deep end again at 30, 35, and you're like, where did my life go? You already know how to cope with that because you haven't built your life to one that you slowly learn to hate. Because for me, I know I can't do that. I will get so depressed so quickly. I'm like, I have to be living a life I love or I just mentally can't handle it. And so...

when those lows come, when those stressors come, I know how to cope with it. And I'm so lucky to be able to have done that at such a young age. And so it doesn't get lost on me that it was not a normal path and that I had so much anger and resentment that I went through so much pain at an early age. But it's a really cool thing as well to know that you've learned how to live your life and cope with your life at an early age and you can go through the rest of your life still learning and adapting,

but you know how to manage it and you have those skills. Exactly. And I think that's something, I think that really breaks my heart though, that a lot of younger people don't have these tools of how to manage, whether it be like depression, anxiety, frustration, or anger, and all of the above. I think a lot of people, they just...

don't know how to cope with it. And that could be because they don't have the funds to get therapy or they are surrounded by family members. Yeah. A lot of times, I mean, it is super expensive and that's why I'm very grateful that, you know, my parents were very supportive. of me kind of going through therapy and getting the help that I needed. But I think one thing that everyone can do is read books because there are so many books that it's like free therapy. There are so many books that really tell you how to cope with your emotions. And I think

we as like a society should be really kind of instilling that into our children at a young age and adding it to our educational education system. Because a lot of times, you know, we don't, we don't have, I guess, the proper education in terms of how to fight those thoughts when you are feeling really down on yourself or how to even think positively about your body and how to have healthy relationships. I think that's a really big one and healthy relationships with yourself.

And even relationally, how do you practice empathy? How do you validate? Like, we are going through like the Black Lives Matter movement right now. And there's so many people that don't know how to say, I see you, I hear you. And I know that I haven't been through the same thing. Like, that's something that... People are having to learn at this point in their lives. And so another thing that kids at that young age, they innately know how to do. They know how to connect and express joy and love and care towards their peers. And we lose that as we grow up because as a society, we're not using those skills. We're not using validation. We're not using empathy. And we're not using kindness as much as we could.

And so I think there's a lot of value that could be given to kids if we just encourage those skills, if we encourage the emotional coping and relationally being effective at a younger age. Exactly. And I think a lot of people, the reason why they have such a hard time with validating people's feelings is because we are often taught that we are right. And it's good to be right. We're taught that if we're wrong, it's a mistake and it's a weakness.

Yes, exactly. And I think we really need to switch the narrative on that one because it's okay if you're wrong. You need to fess up because we all make mistakes. And I really hate the word failure because, I mean, it has such a negative connotation. So I really just like to use the word lesson instead. And I think...

oftentimes we are taught that if we are wrong, we are a failure. And that is not true. I mean, we all make mistakes. We are all wrong at some point. And I think, just learning to really fess up to that and then be able to listen. I think that's a big one too, because a lot of people nowadays, you know, they kind of got their heads in the clouds. It's so easy to just go on your phone, scroll through some things, not even read the entire caption before you comment. I think that's a big one. And kind of just explode on someone that you don't really know. I noticed that.

just in the comment section. I try not to read the comments, to be honest, just for like on big posts, just because I know that's where a lot of negativity breeds. Yeah, it can be very toxic, for sure. Yeah. So for my own personal mental health, I don't really like to read it, but I know that a lot of people just don't even take the time to hear someone out.

and understand their point of view and understand that, you know, we all have different lived experiences and yeah, it can be hard to sometimes understand what someone's been through if you haven't been through it. And sometimes I think that's the most important thing too, that we all just have to realize that we're not always going to understand people. We're not always going to get along, but we should always respect people and just at least try to hear them out, even if you

Yeah, definitely. So what regrets do you have about your college experience? What would you have done differently if you could go back and change anything? One thing that really sticks out at the top of my head, I would say probably the use of daily affirmations, which I know would probably be an interesting regret. I'm sad that I didn't do them sooner, though. I'm a big advocate for

just kind of speaking out loud and speaking your thoughts into fruition. I think that's a super, super, it's just a super important thing because I think there's so many studies too about the act of just speaking. It really kind of, you're able to manifest. And a lot of people think this idea of manifestation and kind of dreaming and dream boards or whatever you want to call it, um,

A lot of people are like, oh, that's so stupid. But I'm like, okay, but it works. It really does work. So I would just say the use of daily affirmations. And I wish I like would manifest more because I think there's something so beautiful that can come out of just like speaking positivity on yourself and others and just kind of.

waking up every day and like I say, I'm strong, I'm confident, I'm powerful and beautiful. And then like just telling yourself that you will have an extraordinary life, even though, I mean, so often it's so easy, especially just, I mean, I would, I would say I'm a pretty average girl. You know, I fit, I, you know, I fit in with the crowd. I get lost in the crowd sometimes, but yeah.
